titulo: How the Spanish Empire Went Broke: The Silver That Wasn't Enough
intro_capitulo: A privateer and the silver fleet
descripcion: It owned the richest silver mountain in the world, and still stopped paying its debts at least nine times between 1557 and 1666. Potosí and the mita, the piece of eight, the price revolution, Philip II's debts and the Great Armada, the expulsion of the Moriscos, the copper vellón cut in half by decree in 1628, and the end: Rocroi, Westphalia and the Pyrenees. Episode two of How Empires Fall. Images: public-domain and freely licensed works from Wikimedia Commons (credits on screen).

escenas.texto: In sixteen twenty eight, off the coast of Cuba, a Dutch privateer named Piet Hein captured the fleet carrying America's silver to Spain. For the king's finances, it was a brutal blow.

And it wasn't the first time the Crown ran out of money. The empire that owned the richest silver mountain on Earth stopped paying its debts at least nine times between fifteen fifty seven and sixteen sixty six.
How does an empire go broke when it was literally digging money out of the ground? This is the story.

visual.src: commons:File:Panorama Villa Imperial de Potosí en 1758 por Gaspar de Berrio.jpg
visual.titulo: HOW THE SPANISH EMPIRE WENT BROKE

escenas.texto: We'll tell it in five parts.
Chapter one. The silver mountain.
In fifteen forty five, in what is now Bolivia, silver was found in a mountain more than four thousand meters high: the Cerro Rico of Potosí.
At its foot grew one of the largest cities in the Americas. This is Potosí in seventeen fifty eight, in a painting by Gaspar de Berrio.

visual.src: commons:File:Panorama Villa Imperial de Potosí en 1758 por Gaspar de Berrio.jpg

escenas.texto: But that silver didn't come out on its own. Thousands of indigenous people were forced to work the mines in shifts, under a system called the mita. Many died doing that work.

visual.src: commons:File:Historia de la conquista del Perú, 1851 "Vista del cerro de Potosí". (3971689798).jpg

escenas.texto: That silver was minted into the piece of eight, a coin that circulated across Europe, the Americas and Asia. Many historians call it the first global currency.
And from every mine, the king took a cut: the royal fifth, twenty percent.

visual.sub: of the silver, for the king

escenas.texto: It looked like the perfect business. But silver had a hidden problem.
Chapter two. More silver, higher prices.
Think about it: if suddenly there's a lot more money, but the same amount of bread, shoes and houses, what happens? Prices go up.

That's what happened in Spain and across Europe for more than a century. Prices rose about one to one and a half percent a year. Today that sounds small, but in an era when prices barely moved, it was a revolution. Historians call it the price revolution.

visual.pre: inflation per year, for over a century

escenas.texto: And the silver didn't stay in Spain. It went to pay armies in Flanders and Italy, and the bankers in Genoa and Augsburg who lent to the king.
Spain had the silver. But much of it ended up in other hands.
Chapter three. The king who didn't pay.
In fifteen fifty six, Charles the Fifth handed the throne to his son, Philip the Second. And along with the throne, he handed him something else: a mountain of debt.

visual.src: commons:File:Anthony van Dyck- Portrait of Charles V on Horseback.JPG
visual.sub: hands over the throne… and the debt

escenas.texto: Philip the Second ruled the largest empire in the world, and he ruled it almost always at war: against France, against the Ottomans, against the rebels in Flanders, and against England.

visual.src: commons:File:King Philip II of Spain, by Sofonisba Anguissola (Museo del Prado, Madrid).jpg

escenas.texto: To pay for it, he borrowed from bankers, mostly Genoese, with short term loans called asientos. And he promised to repay them with silver that would arrive from America.
His debt reached about sixty percent of everything Castile produced in a year.
And four times he stopped paying his bankers: in fifteen fifty seven, fifteen sixty, fifteen seventy five and fifteen ninety six.

the first, just
after taking the throne

escenas.texto: Meanwhile, he was building El Escorial, a huge palace and monastery near Madrid.

visual.src: commons:File:Facade monastery San Lorenzo de El Escorial Spain.jpg

escenas.texto: And in fifteen eighty eight he launched the Great Armada against England: around one hundred forty ships.

visual.src: commons:File:English Ships and the Spanish Armada, August 1588 RMG BHC0262.jpg

escenas.texto: It was a disaster. Between battles and storms, around forty four ships were lost, and between eleven and twenty thousand men died.

visual.src: commons:File:De Spaanse Armada voor de Engelse kust, SK-A-1629.jpg

escenas.texto: Now, an important detail. Several economic historians now think those defaults didn't happen because Spain was ruined, but because of a liquidity problem: the money was coming, just late. The bankers knew it, and kept lending.
The problem is that an empire living on loans against future silver depends on that silver continuing to arrive.

visual.sub: on silver that hasn't arrived yet

escenas.texto: Chapter four. The copper coin.
Philip the Second died in fifteen ninety eight. His son, Philip the Third, inherited the wars, the debts, and in sixteen oh seven, another payment stop.
And between sixteen oh nine and sixteen fourteen he expelled the Moriscos, descendants of Muslims who had converted to Christianity: about three hundred thousand people.
Many were farmers and craftsmen. In regions like Valencia, the hands that worked the land and paid taxes were suddenly gone.

visual.texto: fields with no one to work them

escenas.texto: And to pay the bills, the Crown found a shortcut: minting copper coins, the vellón, and stamping them with whatever value it wanted.

visual.sub: copper coins worth whatever the king said

escenas.texto: It's the same trick we saw in Rome: if there's no silver, you make more coins out of a cheap metal.
But people aren't fools. By sixteen twenty eight, if you wanted to swap copper for silver, you had to pay eighty four percent more. The silver premium reached one point eight four.
And that same year, the king cut the value of copper coins in half by decree. Overnight, anyone holding vellón lost half their money.
It was the same year Piet Hein captured the silver fleet. The year we started with.

visual.sub: silver captured · copper cut in half

escenas.texto: Chapter five. The end.

Philip the Fourth, the king painted by Velázquez, reigned for forty four years, almost all of them at war: the Thirty Years' War in Europe, against the Dutch, against France, and with rebellions in Catalonia and Portugal.

visual.src: commons:File:Diego Rodríguez Velázquez - Felipe IV Rey de España (Prado).jpg

escenas.texto: And he stopped payments in sixteen twenty seven, sixteen forty seven, sixteen fifty two and sixteen sixty two.
In sixteen forty three, at Rocroi, the Spanish tercios, for over a century the most feared infantry in Europe, suffered a crushing defeat against France.

visual.sub: the myth of the tercios falls

escenas.texto: In sixteen forty eight came the Peace of Westphalia, and with it, Spain recognized Dutch independence after eighty years of war.
And in sixteen fifty nine, with the Peace of the Pyrenees, France took Spain's place as Europe's great power.
The empire lasted a long time after that, especially in the Americas. But its era of dominance in Europe was over.
See the pattern? It's the same as Rome. One: spend far more on wars than comes in. Two: plug the hole with debt. And three: when that's not enough, mess with the money.

items.texto: Wars that cost more than comes in
When it's not enough: mess with the money

escenas.texto: And Spain leaves an even stranger lesson: having silver is not the same as being rich. A country's wealth is in what it produces, not in the metal it digs out of the ground.
That was episode two of How Empires Fall. Comment which empire you want next, and subscribe so you don't miss it.
